title: Design And Development Of A Web-Based Digital Credit Service And Qris Transaction System
summary: The rapid development of financial technology (fintech) has accelerated the adoption of digital payment and digital credit services. However, most digital credit services still rely on cash disbursement mechanisms, making it difficult to control the utilization of borrowed funds. This study aims to develop PayQRIS, a web-based Buy Now, Pay Later (PayLater) service integrated with QRIS payments that enables cashless transactions using credit limits without direct cash disbursement. The system was developed using the Prototyping model and evaluated through black-box testing and the System Usability Scale (SUS). The results show that PayQRIS successfully integrates PayLater services with QRIS payments into a single platform featuring credit limit determination, installment and bill management, bill extension, and secure transaction authentication. Functional testing confirmed that all system features operated according to the specified requirements, while the usability evaluation produced a SUS score of 83.25, indicating a high level of usability and user acceptance. Therefore, PayQRIS provides a web-based PayLater solution that supports QRIS payments through a more controlled digital credit mechanism.

title: Levels of AI Investment, Environmental Disclosure Performance, and Firms’ Interest-Bearing Debt Financing Levels
summary: Due to the broad use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in enterprises’ operations, an issue arises regarding the influence of AI investments on the financing behavior of firms. In this study, a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2023 was used to empirically investigate the influence of AI investment levels on interest-bearing debt ratios of firms, as well as to test the role of environmental disclosure performance in this regard. The results show that there exists a strong positive relationship between AI investment levels and interest-bearing debt ratios, which might mean either a high propensity to finance through debt or higher interest-bearing debts of firms. According to the results of stepwise regression, it can be concluded that AI investments are negatively related to environmental disclosure performance, and environmental disclosure performance is negatively correlated with interest-bearing debt ratios of firms, suggesting resource trade-offs. Heterogeneity analysis shows that this effect is mainly valid for large-scale firms, and robustness tests confirm the main results of this paper.

title: Machine Learning Meets Blockchain: A Domain-Oriented Review of Integration Mechanisms, Applications and Open Challenges
summary: Blockchain and machine learning (ML) are combined in systems that must learn from multi-party data and keep a verifiable record of what was used and decided. This scoping-style review of a ranked sample covers seven domains: healthcare, finance, supply chain, energy, smart contracts, transportation and education. We searched Scopus and IEEE Xplore on 15 October 2026, ranked 5,195 candidate records, read 345 abstracts in rank order, coded a core corpus of 192 studies and read 38 in full. Federated learning is the most common method (93 of 192 core studies name it), and detection of fraud, intrusions and vulnerabilities is the most common task among the 38. None of the 38 reports a deployment, 24 report a measured ledger figure and two measure ledger energy. Ten use more than one privacy mechanism, and only two report accuracy with and without it. Attack tests are small, and one study tests a Sybil attacker. Studies differ too much to compare, so we do not rank domains. A ledger shows that a record has not changed, not that it was correct when written. The main gaps are realistic evaluation, shared benchmarks and reporting standards, and tested explanations for decisions made inside contracts.

title: The Effect of Financial Reporting Transparency on Audit Report Quality in Kenyan Public Universities
summary: This study examined the effect of financial reporting transparency on audit report quality in Kenyan public universities. The quality of audit reports in Kenyan public universities remains a concern due to inadequate financial disclosures, incomplete reporting, and limited accessibility of financial information, which undermine audit reliability and institutional accountability. Anchored on Agency Theory, the study adopted a positivist research philosophy and a cross-sectional research design. The target population comprised 175 respondents, representing five respondents from each of the 35 publicly chartered universities, including finance officers, internal auditors, accountants, and audit or finance committee members. Institutional census and purposive sampling techniques were employed. Four universities outside the target population participated in the pilot study. Primary data were collected using structured questionnaires, while secondary data were obtained from published audit reports and financial statements. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression. Findings indicated moderately high financial reporting transparency (M = 3.63, SD = 1.24) and a positive, statistically significant relationship with audit report quality (r = 0.612, p < 0.01; ? = 0.598, p < 0.05), explaining 37.5 per cent of its variation (R² = 0.375). The study concluded that transparent financial reporting facilitates reliable audit assessments by ensuring the availability of complete, timely, and accessible financial information. It recommends strengthening disclosure requirements and financial reporting practices to enhance audit credibility. The findings provide evidence to inform financial reporting policies, strengthen institutional oversight, and promote accountability in Kenyan public universities.

title: A essencialidade do serviço público diante das transformações digitais e do orçamento escasso: a estabilidade como garantia de continuidade das políticas públicas de saúde e educação
summary: This article analyzes the essential nature of public service in the face of digital transformations and budgetary constraints confronting Public Administration in Brazil, from the perspective of a State fit for the 21st century. It is a qualitative, exploratory study based on a review of legal doctrine, legislation, and case law regarding civil servant tenure. The study concludes that digital transformations and budgetary constraints pose significant challenges to Public Administration but do not diminish the importance of public service or the need to maintain a workforce of tenured civil servants.

title: Data privacy and audit compliance of supply chain finance warehouse receipt pledge based on WSN federated edge learning
summary: Abstract In supply chain finance warehouse receipt pledge financing, the status of the pledged assets is difficult to verify in real time, the risk of privacy leakage of financing data is high, and the federal training process lacks verifiable audit trajectories for regulatory authorities. To achieve multi-warehouse collaborative risk control modeling under the condition of data not leaving the domain and meet the requirements of privacy protection and audit compliance, a method for privacy and audit compliance of supply chain finance warehouse receipt pledge data based on federated edge learning of wireless sensor networks is constructed. A pledge perception and digital warehouse receipt generation mechanism based on wireless sensor networks is designed. A federated edge learning architecture integrating trust and energy-aware weighted aggregation, federated proximal terms and communication compression is constructed. The study introduces a joint security aggregation mechanism of differential privacy and homomorphic encryption, as well as an audit compliance framework for blockchain smart contracts. The experimental results show that when the data heterogeneity parameter is 0.1, the test accuracy of the proposed method reaches 88.4%, which is 9.9% higher than the 78.5% of the federal average algorithm. In the ablation experiment, the F1 score of the complete method is 93.6%, while it drops to 88.9% after removing the federal proximal term. When the privacy budget is 0.10, the accuracy rate of the proposed method is 92.1%, which is 8.0% higher than the 84.1% of the federal average algorithm. The results show that the proposed method has stronger robustness under extreme non-independent homogeneous distribution conditions. Trust and energy-aware selection and federated proximal terms contribute significantly to accuracy, and the privacy enhancement mechanism achieves effective privacy protection with limited accuracy loss. This research provides a technical path that takes into account data privacy, model performance and audit compliance for the warehouse receipt pledge scenario in supply chain finance, which is conducive to promoting the compliant application of federated learning in supply chain finance risk control.

title: Beyond Spending: Towards a Need-Based and Equity-Driven Framework for CSR Allocation in India
summary: The mandatory implementation of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, has institutionalized a steady stream of private capital into India’s social development ecosystem. However, over a decade of empirical spending trends reveals severe structural, geographical, and sectoral disparities. Driven by compliance mandates and operational proximity, corporate capital flows disproportionately toward industrially advanced states and urban clusters. Conversely, socio-economically vulnerable areas—including aspirational districts, tribal belts, rural hinterlands, and climate-fragile regions—remain chronically underfunded. This paper critically examines the limitations of the current proximity-focused and compliance-driven CSR paradigm. To reconcile corporate preferences with national equity goals, this study proposes an evidence-based, need-driven allocation framework. By operationalizing objective multi-dimensional metrics—such as district-level Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) scores, Human Development Index (HDI) parameters, Aspirational District rankings, and climate vulnerability indices—the proposed model enables corporate boards to target high-need intervention zones where social capital produces the highest marginal utility. Ultimately, the paper advocates for a fundamental shift in evaluating CSR performance, moving from input-based financial compliance to outcome-oriented metrics centered on spatial equity and long-term socio-economic impact.

title: The Income Stability Premium (ISP): A Unique Revenue Model for Gig Economy Workers
summary: Anyone who has spent a week talking to a delivery partner or a cab driver in Bengaluru will have heard the same complaint. It is not that the money is bad. It is that the money is unpredictable. A festival week can bring in twice what a rainy week does, and the rent, the EMI on the bike and the school fees do not care which kind of week it was. Salaried people get a predictable credit on the last day of the month, and a whole financial system is built around that predictability. Gig workers get none of it. This matters because the group is no longer small. NITI Aayog (2022) estimated that about 7.7 million Indians worked in the gig economy in 2020-21 and expected the number to reach 23.5 million by 2029-30. Karnataka went a step further in 2025 by passing a dedicated law for platform workers, which requires aggregators to pay a welfare fee of between 1% and 5% of each payout (Government of Karnataka, 2025). In short, a large and growing group of earners has an income pattern that mainstream finance still handles badly. For this proposal, I have designed a revenue model for a finance product aimed at exactly this gap. The product is called SteadyPay, a service that turns a gig worker's bumpy weekly earnings into a steady monthly payout. The revenue model behind it is what I have named the Income Stability Premium (ISP) Model. Instead of earning money by charging interest on loans, SteadyPay earns a small premium for taking on the worker's income volatility, and the premium rises or falls with how volatile that worker's income actually is. Note on Assumptions: Assumptions are marked as such wherever they appear. The main ones are: (1) SteadyPay is run by a fintech company that partners with an RBI-regulated NBFC, which actually books the advances, so the RBI (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025 apply in full; (2) every figure on volumes, costs and loss rates is an illustrative assumption for a 10,000-worker cohort and not observed data; (3) workers earn through platforms that can share payout data with the worker's consent; (4) the average worker in the cohort earns about Rs. 24,000 a month; and (5) all amounts are in Indian rupees (Rs.) and tax effects are ignored for simplicity. The Proposed Model: Income Stability Premium (ISP) The ISP Model rests on one idea: predictability is a product, and it can be priced. A worker who earns Rs. 24,000 on average but swings between Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 31,000 is, in effect, carrying a risk. SteadyPay offers to carry that risk for a fee. The worker gets a fixed payout every month (the Steady Payout). The fee (the Stability Premium) is a percentage of that payout, and the percentage depends on how volatile the worker's earnings have been over the last six months. How SteadyPay Works The flow is simple enough to explain to a driver in one minute. The worker links one or more platform accounts and gives consent for payout data to be shared. SteadyPay studies the last six months of earnings and offers a Steady Payout set at roughly 80-85% of the average. Platform payouts are routed to a ring-fenced escrow account in the worker's name. Each month the Steady Payout goes to the worker's bank account on a fixed date, and whatever earnings are left after the premium go into a Stability Pool. The Pool belongs to the worker and acts as a cushion. In a weak month the Pool tops up the payout. If the Pool runs dry, SteadyPay advances the gap from its partner NBFC's funds, and that advance is recovered from later surplus. Revenue Streams and Pricing The ISP Model has one main revenue stream and two small supporting ones: • Stability Premium (main stream): 0.9% blended on an average Steady Payout of Rs. 20,000 gives Rs. 180 per worker a month, or Rs. 2,160 a year. • Platform integration fee: Platforms benefit when their partners stay on board; I assume they pay Rs. 12 per worker per month for the data connection and payout routing (Rs. 144 a year). • Protection commissions: Optional accident cover at Rs. 60 a month, with 30% opting in and a 20% commission, adds about Rs. 43 per worker a year. Unit Economics and Break-Even Tested on a cohort of 10,000 active workers, revenue works out to about Rs. 2,347 per worker annually. Variable costs are about Rs. 1,235 (cost of funds, credit losses at 0.15%, customer support, and replacing 40% annual churn), leaving a contribution of roughly Rs. 1,112 per worker. Dividing fixed costs of Rs. 2.5 crore by the contribution gives a break-even of around 22,500 active workers. At 50,000 workers, revenue reaches Rs. 11.74 crore and operating profit hits about Rs. 3.06 crore (a 26% margin). Why This Model Is Unique The products closest to SteadyPay are earned wage access and small gig worker loans, both priced on amount borrowed and duration. ISP differs in three ways: 1. Prices volatility itself, not the loan: Workers pay for the guarantee even if they never take an advance. 2. The buffer is the worker's own money: The Stability Pool is built from surplus months. 3. Price falls as income steadies: Incentivizes multi-platform work or regular habits. 2.6 Practicality, Sustainability & Risk Management • Regulation: Must operate via bank/NBFC partnerships ensuring compliance with RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025) and transparent APR disclosures. • Advantages: Provides predictable income for workers, boosts retention for platforms, offers recurring fee income for the fintech provider, and promotes financial inclusion. • Disadvantages & Mitigation: Adverse selection (mitigated by 6-month history requirements), moral hazard (mitigated by setting payouts below average income), dependency on platform data (mitigated by bank-account/Account Aggregator integration), and scale requirements. Conclusion The Income Stability Premium Model starts from the observation that the real financial problem for many gig workers is unpredictability, not just income shortage. SteadyPay prices this predictability so the company earns by absorbing volatility rather than lending at high interest. While sensitive to loss rates and premium sizing, it provides a viable, sustainable path toward financial stability for a rapidly expanding workforce segment. References • Government of Karnataka. title: Segurança de dados e turismo modelo teórico de práticas de responsabilidade social corporativa e cibersegurança em Travel Techs
summary: Technological resources enable companies to increase their competitiveness, communication and sales. In tourism, Travel Techs apply innovative technologies to optimize the traveler experience and, in a way, help companies to obtain technology in their daily lives, improving internal processes. The use of the internet and technologies has become important for the expansion of sales channels, but their use has risks, including data breaches and leaks, mainly because they involve financial data of customers and companies. Given the scenario of cybersecurity and data protection, which shows that companies need to protect themselves in order to guarantee quality services, the use of corporate social responsibility (CSR) linked to cybersecurity seeks to recognize the challenges inherent to data breaches and leaks that tourism companies face in maintaining the quality of their services, protecting their data and that of their customers, in addition to protecting the company's image. CSR in the context of cybersecurity has several benefits for Travel Techs that adopt its nuances, since the absence of data breaches or leaks affects the company's image, thus creating a solid reputation in the market. Travel Techs that prioritize data security have provided a secure environment for their customers and protected themselves from potential breaches. Therefore, this article aims to propose a theoretical model that explores the intersection of CSR best practices and cybersecurity in the context of Travel Techs.

title: Restricted Equity Incentive and Stock Price Crash Risk: Evidence from China A-share Listed Companies
summary: This study takes China A-share listed companies in 2012-2022 as samples to test the impact of restricted equity incentives on the risk of stock price crash. Using the two-way fixed effect and DID method, we find that the implementation of restricted equity incentive significantly increases the risk of stock price collapse, which can be measured by negative skewness coefficient (NCSKEW) and bottom-up volatility (DUVOL). After parallel trend test, tendency score matching (PSM-DID) and including lagging dependent variables, the baseline results are still robust, and the effects are dynamically accumulated after implementation. Heterogeneity analysis shows that this effect is more obvious in state-owned enterprises, large enterprises, high-growth enterprises, enterprises with concentrated ownership and enterprises with higher profits. These findings show that restrictive equity incentives may aggravate the short-term behavior of management and the hoarding of bad news, thus increasing the possibility of collapse. This study contributes to the literature of equity incentives and provides enlightenment for corporate governance and regulatory policies in emerging markets.

title: Characteristics of Innovative Digital Technology Entrepreneurship in South Africa: Case of KwaZulu-Natal
summary: This study examines entrepreneurial characteristics of innovative digital technology entrepreneurship in Kwa-Zulu Natal, for survival and growth. These characteristics are in two folds: personal traits and entrepreneurial behaviour. The purpose of these objective is to address innovative digital SMEs in South Africa who often either struggle to effectively use digital systems such as computers and software’s, or they completely lack adequate skills to exploit the benefits of the digital technology. A quantitative research approach was adopted, while using a non-probability sampling technique to achieve a sample size of 179 excluding 10 participants for pilot study. Data were collected using a self-administered, closed-ended questionnaire, with predetermined answers scaled using a 5-point Likert scale, while data analysis was conducted using SPSS (version 29.0). Innovative digital technology entrepreneurship is becoming recognised worldwide for its significant positive impact on the economic and social growth of a country. It is an important driver for economic growth and development in South Africa. Nevertheless, the study found that digital SMEs in undeveloped and small communities in South Africa have significant constraints that affect both the survival and growth in these regions. Thus, this paper aims to identify key areas whereentrepreneurial characteristics impacts innovative digital technology entrepreneurship. The study also found that the primary factors that are contributing to the failure of innovative digital technology entrepreneurship is the lack of entrepreneurial passion and intention. This involves willingness to adapt to the ever-changing technology and lack of technical adequacy and flexibility to digital transformation especially in underdeveloped areas of South Africa. Hence, this this study recommends that the innovative digital entrepreneurs must elevate their level of technical skills and entrepreneurial characteristics they possess in order to adapt quickly to the digital transformation.

title: Gender Hierarchies in the Fast Fashion Industry: The Role of Exploitative Labor Practices in Perpetuating Gender Inequality
summary: Fast fashion has become a global phenomenon, yet few people recognize the industry's reliance on the exploitation of women, who make up the majority of its workforce. This thesis examines how the labor practices of the fast fashion industry reinforce gender inequality, with a focus on Bangladesh and other major garment-producing countries. By tracing the economic, social, and historical forces that have driven the feminization of garment labor, this project demonstrates how the industry perpetuates systemic gendered exploitation through low wages, dangerous working conditions, and gender-based violence. Grounded in feminist labor theory, Marxist critiques, and globalization frameworks, this project situates the fast fashion industry within the broader intersection of capitalism, patriarchy, and globalization. A case study of Bangladeshi garment worker protests exemplifies how the fast fashion business model exacerbates gendered exploitation, while an analysis of corporate social responsibility efforts and worker resistance movements assesses both challenges and opportunities for reform. By contextualizing the relationship between gender, labor, and power, this thesis aims to expose the contradiction between fast fashion's feminist marketing strategies and the exploitation of its female workers, ultimately advocating for change toward a more equitable and ethical fashion industry.

title: Financial investors and for-profit providers as new players in global healthcare: the politics and practices of health system financialisation
summary: Private for-profit providers and internationally operating financial investors are gaining influence in health systems around the world.Governments of tax-funded national systems (NHS) and social health insurance systems have historically been reluctant to let for-profit actors operate within them.Many now welcome private equity (PE), venture capital and institutional investors as sources of capital and as providers of rapid solutions to pressing policy concerns such as workforce shortages.Examples include the role of private providers in addressing long waiting lists for hospital or nursing home care, and the development of digital infrastructure for technologyenabled home care.Proponents argue that private capital fills funding gaps that public budgets cannot.Critics point to the risks for costs, quality, and system stability and ask how the interests of patients and healthcare workers can be placed above, or at least alongside, those of shareholders.To gain an understanding of how for-profit providers and financial investors operate within domestic health systems and across national borders, we organised a workshop with the Commonwealth Fund of New York and the Health Policy and Management Department at Columbia University in New York City in May 2025.European observers often regard the United States (US) as the birthplace of healthcare capitalism and look across the Atlantic for evidence on what financial ownership does to health outcomes and expenditure.Yet the rapid entry and consolidation of financial actors is an evolving policy challenge in the US too, with many unknowns, not least because financial (trans)actions are fast moving and volatile.American policy experts and scholars, in turn, look to Europe for regulatory strategies.The workshop brought policy experts, clinicians, and PE representatives together with a large group of international scholars, and we invited participants to write comparative papers on the role of for-profit providers and financial investors across health systems.Several of the resulting author teams had never written together, and some had not met before the workshop.The collaborations produced informed and searching debate, and this special issue of Health Economics Policy and Law publishes the results.Alongside perspective articles and research papers, the issue includes a paper based on an expert panel we hosted in July 2026, in which Professor David Blumenthal, Professor Erin Fuse Brown, and Rob Coppedge discussed how financial actors are gaining ground in US healthcare, how this affects traditional, profession-based arrangements for organising care, and where the opportunities for regulation lie.The full panel discussion is available on the website of Health Economics Policy and Law.

title: Beyond the Power Law: Log-Normal Bodies, Pareto Tails, and the Limits of Industry Statistics
summary: Background: The claim that a power law governs the distribution of value in a digital economy is usually asserted about sectors, while the evidence for heavy tails concerns firms. The two are different objects, and the claim is rarely tested at the level at which it is made. Methods: We test it at three levels using two censuses: every US employer firm from 1978 to 2023 in ten published size classes and 71 industries in the national accounts from 1997 to 2025. Distributions are fitted to interval-censored counts by maximum likelihood and compared by Vuong’s test; the tail is located by a threshold sweep; concentration from grouped data is bounded rather than estimated. Results: A log-normal is preferred over a Pareto in all forty-six years, yet underpredicts the number of firms with 10,000 employees or more by a factor of twenty-one, so the distribution is a mixture whose tail alone is consistent with a power law. When refitted with more than twenty employees, the exponent is 1.056, within three thousandths of a published microdata estimate obtained by a different method. Between sectors, the claim fails on two tests: industry scale carries no information about the share of value an industry retains, with correlations of 0.009 (Pearson) and −0.047 (Spearman), and the rise in the large-firm employment share is not compositional, since employment moved toward less concentrated sectors throughout. Conclusions: The power law operates on firms within industries, in the tail, which is where every instrument used here stops resolving differences. Rejecting a sectoral power law does not refute firm-level winner-take-all; it places that phenomenon below the resolution of the public statistics in which the debate is usually conducted.

title: Research on the Motivation and Performance of Green Investment by Listed Companies in Shaanxi Province
summary: China actively advocates the construction of an ecological civilization. As one of the key instruments for promoting ecological civilization, green investment plays a vital role in solving resource and environmental problems and in building an energy-saving, emissions-reducing, clean and low-carbon production and living system[1]. As an important energy base of China, Shaanxi Province's exploration and practice of green investment by its listed companies is not only related to the green transformation of the regional economy, but also plays an exemplary role in green development nationwide[2]. This study focuses on the green investment behavior of listed companies in Shaanxi and aims to reveal the motivations behind it and its performance effects. The paper reviews the background and significance of green investment research, integrates domestic and international research results, introduces the current situation of green investment development of listed companies in Shaanxi, and analyzes in depth the key factors affecting green investment decisions, such as market competition pressure, environmental regulation policies, and corporate social responsibility[3]. Through empirical research methods, the paper not only tests the direct impact of green investment on the economic performance of enterprises, but also explores its long-term impact on environmental performance[4]. Finally, based on the empirical results, targeted green investment strategy suggestions are put forward for listed companies in Shaanxi Province[5].

title: DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURES AND LOGISTICS ACTIVITIES IN SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT OF RETAIL FIRMS IN CROSS RIVER STATE
summary: This study examines the influence of digital infrastructures and logistics activities on sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) of retail firms in Cross River State, Nigeria. Against the backdrop of fast-tracking digital transformation across African retail ecosystem and the growing need for sustainability integration in business logistics, this research interrogates how cloud computing, Internet of Things (IoT), blockchain technology, enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, and digital logistics platforms collectively shape the sustainability performance of retail supply chains in an emerging economy. This research is anchored on the Resource-Based View (RBV) theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework, the study adopted a quantitative cross-sectional survey research design. A structured questionnaire was administered to 300 purposively and randomly selected managers and logistics officers from registered retail firms in Calabar, Ogoja, and Ikom metropolis. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlation, and multiple regression analysis via SPSS version 26. Findings revealed that digital infrastructure adoption (β = .387, p < .001), logistics technology integration (β = .271, p < .001), and supply chain transparency (β = .201, p = .001) jointly and significantly predict sustainable supply chain management, accounting for 61.5% of its variance (R² = .615, F(3,296) = 158.34, p < .001). The study concludes that robust digital infrastructure deployment and technologically driven logistics operations serve as critical enablers of economic, environmental, and social sustainability in the retail sector of Cross River State. It recommends that retail firms invest strategically in scalable digital platforms, collaborative logistics networks, and technology-driven transparency mechanisms, while state governments should strengthen broadband infrastructure and create enabling policy frameworks for digital commerce in Nigeria's south-south geopolitical zone. Keywords: Digital Infrastructure, Logistics Activities, Sustainable Supply Chain Management, Retail Firms, Cross River State, Nigeria, Digital Transformation, Triple Bottom Line.

title: The authorisation of crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) in the EU under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR)
summary: As its title denotes, this study develops on the authorisation of crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) in the European Union (EU) under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR). It is structured in three Sections as follows: Section A develops on the relevant provisions of MiCAR relating to the conditions for a person to be allowed to provide crypto-asset services within the EU and the single passport regime (Article 59), as well as the application for authorisation (Article 62 and the related Delegated and Implementing Regulations), and the assessment of that application by national competent authorities (NCAs), leading to the granting or refusal of authorisation (Article 63) in accordance with the “three step” procedure set out in these two Articles. The focus of Section B turns to some specific related provisions, namely, the governance arrangements under Article 68 and the identification, prevention, management and disclosure of conflicts of interest under Article 72. Read together with Articles 62-63, these Articles reflect the MiCAR’s emphasis on effective corporate governance, sound risk management and the mitigation of conflicts of interest as essential safeguards for the provision of crypto-asset services. The concluding remarks are included in Section C.

title: Institutional and organizational framework for implementing strategic priorities of the development of Ukraine’s logistics information and telecommunication system
summary: The article substantiates the theoretical, legal, and managerial foundations for establishing an institutional environment to support the implementation of strategic priorities for developing Ukraine’s Logistics Information and Telecommunication System (LITS) under conditions of martial law and post-war economic recovery. The study conceptualizes the multi-level institutional architecture of LITS as a coherent system integrating national, interdepartmental, regional, sector-specific, and corporate governance tiers. The methodological framework includes institutional analysis, systematic structural synthesis, evolutionary modeling, and scenario management. The analysis shows that implementing LITS target parameters requires clear distribution of authority among market participants, aligned inter-agency interaction protocols, multi-channel investment allocation, and robust cybersecurity protocols. The paper systematizes Ukraine’s regulatory foundation, including national economic, regional, and transport strategies, as well as legal acts governing multimodal transport, electronic documentation, and cybersecurity. International best practices (EU, USA, Japan, South Korea, China) in managing logistics digitalization are analyzed. The study highlights the relevance of adapting the European Union’s eFTI regulation, TEN-T corridor management, and digital single-window frameworks to guarantee seamless interoperability with EU transport networks. The author develops a multi-tiered institutional model centered around a unified decentralized logistics data contour. This model connects public-private partnerships, national registries, and analytical platforms with iterative feedback loops for continuous monitoring, risk assessment, and scenario adjustment. Keywords: institutional framework, logistics information and telecommunication system, digital transformation, European integration, decentralized data contour, multimodal transport, supply chain resilience, scenario management.

title: Current strategies for financing enterprise development: an innovative and harmonious approach
summary: This article examines corporate financial development through innovative and harmonious approaches. The main trend in the development of corporate financial structures is the use of financial technologies that accelerate investment attraction and increase the transparency of financial transactions. This paper examines one of the latest tools for the financial sector’s digital transformation: the tokenization of real assets. This mechanism provides access to new investment opportunities, allowing enterprises to transfer their assets into the digital realm and trade them on relevant markets to attract additional funding. The paper also examines ESG financing, which integrates environmental, social, and governance criteria into investment and financial decision-making. The paper establishes that implementing ESG principles enables companies to attract financial resources through specialized sustainable financing mechanisms, namely green bonds, social bonds, sustainable development bonds, ESG loans, and investments by specialized ESG funds. This paper examines the trend toward the digital transformation of financial management, which involves implementing artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies to streamline business processes and improve analytical capabilities and decision-making efficiency. The paper examines crowdfunding and venture capital as innovative mechanisms for raising funds from investors via specialized online platforms at various stages of a company’s development. Innovative opportunities for the financial and harmonious development of enterprises hold significant potential for further advancement through digitalization—specifically by leveraging cutting-edge platforms to attract investment, manage accounting, and monitor processes. title: Enterprise AI Supply Chain Security and Model Provenance Framework
summary: Enterprise AI solutions depend on complex supply chains that include foundation models, open-source libraries, datasets, embeddings, model hubs, APIs, containers, prompts, retrieval components, plugins, agent tools, and third-party services. Weaknesses or tampering anywhere in this chain can introduce security, integrity, licensing, privacy, and operational risks. This paper proposes an Enterprise AI Supply Chain Security and Model Provenance Framework that combines asset inventory, trusted sourcing, software and model bills of materials, provenance metadata, cryptographic integrity, vulnerability management, dependency analysis, provider assurance, artifact signing, environment controls, and continuous monitoring. The framework defines controls across acquisition, development, training, fine-tuning, deployment, update, and retirement. It also addresses model lineage, dataset lineage, prompt provenance, external tools, agent dependencies, and evidence for audit and incident response. The proposed approach enables enterprises to verify what AI components are used, where they originated, how they changed, and whether they remain trusted throughout the lifecycle.

title: The Digital Europe Programme: Türkiye’s Expectations and Contributions to the Programme
summary: Digitalization has played a significant role in the relationship between the European Union and Türkiye since the beginning of the 2000s. It constitutes a significant component of strategic economic and technological cooperation beyond the political vision of the European Union (EU). Türkiye either participates as a partner in the European Union’s digital transformation programs in line with its objectives of economic development and technological advancement, or closely monitors these processes. Research on the Digital Europe programme remains quite limited, and there is no study that specifically examines Türkiye’s position in this programme. The programme specifically focuses on the key issues of contemporary digital transformation, with objectives including artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, cybersecurity, digital skills, semiconductors, and digital capacity building. The objectives of the programme, the expectations of Türkiye and its potential contributions are the main research questions. It utilizes the document analysis technique to analyze data from EU documents, records of video conferences organized by the Directorate for EU Affairs, and official websites. This study explains the opportunities for Türkiye, and emphasizes the importance of broader and deeper participation in the programme. Moreover, it highlights Türkiye’s impact on the achievement of the EU’s programme objectives.

title: E-Governance and Socio-Economic Development in Nasarawa State, Nigeria
summary: The growing use of information and communication technologies (ICTs) in public administration has transformed how governments deliver services and interact with citizens. However, despite Nigeria’s increasing investment in digital governance, questions remain about whether e-governance has generated meaningful socio-economic benefits at the state level. This study examined the impact of e-governance on socio-economic development in Nasarawa State, Nigeria. Guided by the Technological Determinism Theory, the study adopted a mixed-methods research design. Primary data were collected through questionnaires administered to 395 respondents and interviews with 13 key participants, while secondary data were obtained from relevant literature and official documents. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, whereas qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. The findings indicate that e-governance has improved access to public services, enhanced administrative efficiency, increased transparency, and encouraged participation in the digital economy. Nevertheless, these gains are limited by poor internet connectivity, unreliable electricity supply, low digital literacy, and inadequate ICT infrastructure, particularly in rural communities. The study concludes that while e-governance has positively influenced socio-economic development in Nasarawa State, addressing infrastructural and institutional barriers is essential to fully realise its developmental potential. It therefore recommends greater investment in ICT infrastructure and electricity supply, and improved digital literacy.

title: Urban ecological resilience and industrial structure optimization coupling coordination in the Beibu Gulf Urban Agglomeration
summary: The synergy of industrial transformation and ecological security is an important pair in the regional high-quality development. Previous studies of the Beibu Gulf Urban Agglomeration have mainly examined industrial development, ecological carrying capacity, low-carbon transition, or environmental resilience separately, leaving the coordinated evolution of industrial structure optimization and urban ecological resilience insufficiently understood. This gap is particularly relevant for late-developing coastal urban agglomerations, where rapid industrial restructuring occurs alongside increasing ecological pressures. To address this issue, taking the Beibu Gulf Urban Agglomeration as the study area, an evaluation system for industrial structure optimization and urban ecological resilience was constructed, and the coupling coordination between the two systems was examined from 2012 to 2022. The contribution of this study lies in integrating industrial structure optimization (ISO) and urban ecological resilience (UER) within a unified analytical framework and simultaneously examining their temporal evolution, spatial differentiation, subsystem-lagging characteristics, and interacting driving factors. The findings extend the empirical understanding of industrial–ecological coordination in late-developing coastal urban agglomerations and provide a quantitative basis for differentiated sustainability governance. Results indicate that the industrial structure optimization and the urban ecological resilience had steadily improved over the study period, however, there remained large inter-city variation. The average coupling coordination degree rose from 0.338 in 2012 to 0.432 in 2022, which reflects the changing trend of mild disorder-to-near-order but overall systems still not into the coordinated development stages. At the spatial level, the coordination pattern was featured with a remarkable core, higher values in northern regions and differentiated performance among coastal port cities. Nanning booth performed as a leader city and FangchengGang better Chongzuo always weak. The results of the geographical detector show that development of digital economyhas a dominant explanatory power on gross regional environmental quality, followed by science–technology input, economic development, transport accessibility and environmental regulation. The results of interaction detection indicate that the synergistic effect of digital economy and science-technology input has the strongest explanatory power. These findings identify the major factors and interaction patterns associated with spatial differences in industrial–ecological coordination and provide quantitative evidence for differentiated governance in late-developing coastal urban agglomerations.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Accounting Performance: Examining Accounting Efficiency, Financial Reporting Quality and Managerial Decision-Making
summary: The rapid adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming accounting practices by influencing how financial information is processed, reported, and used for managerial decision-making. However, limited empirical evidence explains how GenAI adoption and accounting efficiency jointly contribute to accounting performance, particularly through financial reporting quality. This study therefore examines the relationships among Generative Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Accounting Efficiency, Financial Reporting Quality, and Accounting Performance within an integrated accounting framework. The study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional approach using data collected from 250 accounting and finance professionals. The relationships among the constructs were examined using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0. The findings indicate that Generative AI Adoption has a positive effect on Accounting Performance and Financial Reporting Quality, while Accounting Efficiency also has positive effects on both outcomes. Financial Reporting Quality demonstrates a strong positive effect on Accounting Performance and further serves as an important mediating mechanism between Generative AI Adoption and Accounting Performance, as well as between Accounting Efficiency and Accounting Performance. The structural model indicates that the proposed relationships provide meaningful explanatory and predictive value for the endogenous constructs. Overall, the findings suggest that the benefits of Generative AI in accounting extend beyond automation and become more meaningful when AI adoption is supported by efficient accounting processes and high-quality financial reporting. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI and accounting by providing an integrated perspective on how technological adoption, accounting efficiency, and financial reporting quality can collectively strengthen accounting performance and support managerial decision-making.

title: Branding in the Digital Era: IGSB's Social Media Analysis
summary: The digital transformation of higher education has changed how institutions communicate their identity, engage stakeholders and build brand visibility. This study examines the social media branding practices of Indira Global School of Business (IGSB), Pune, focusing on the nature and distribution of its published content. Using a descriptive case-study approach, IGSB’s social media communication from 21 August 2023 to September 2026 was analysed. During this period IGSB recorded 1,001 posts; a structured dataset of 176 posts was classified into eight thematic categories: Academic, Student Experience, Industry Connect, Admissions, Achievements, Institutional, Cultural/Social, and Brand/Creative. Cultural/Social content formed the largest category (30.68%), followed by Academic (23.30%) and Student Experience (22.16%) content. Industry Connect accounted for 8.52% and Institutional content for 5.68%, while Achievements and Admissions each represented 4.55%. The findings suggest that IGSB’s digital brand communication extends beyond conventional promotion and increasingly represents the institution through its academic environment, student experiences, cultural identity and industry engagement. The study demonstrates how systematic content classification can give educational institutions a practical framework for evaluating their digital brand-building activities.

title: Corporate Greenwashing-Oriented Pseudo-Innovation: A Literature Review
summary: Against the backdrop of China's dual-carbon goals and the rapid expansion of ESG disclosure requirements, the volume of corporate green innovation has risen sharply. At the same time, more formalistic and strategic forms of innovation have appeared, often taking green patents and R&D expenditure as visible signs of environmental commitment. Drawing on both Chinese- and English-language studies, this review examines greenwashing-oriented pseudo-innovation from four perspectives: conceptual meaning, antecedents, economic consequences, and governance. Particular attention is paid to the boundary between this form of pseudo-innovation and conventional verbal greenwashing or broader forms of pseudo-corporate social responsibility. The review also summarizes theoretical developments and empirical evidence, identifies unresolved issues in conceptualization, identification and measurement, and governance, and outlines directions for future research. Existing studies suggest that greenwashing-oriented pseudo-innovation is an opportunistic strategy in which apparently substantive innovative actions are used as a symbolic vehicle to obtain legitimacy-related benefits. Such behavior can weaken market trust, damage corporate reputation, and distort the allocation of resources intended for genuine green innovation. Further work is therefore needed to sharpen the concept, improve measurement, and develop more targeted governance mechanisms.

title: How Far Can Regulation Be Simplified? Decriminalisation, Facilitation and Accountability under the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
summary: Every reform walks a tightrope between freedom and control. The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which the Union Finance Minister, Nirmala Sitharaman, placed before the Lok Sabha on 23 March 2026, walks that tightrope at national scale. It is among the widest revisions of India’s company law framework since the Companies Act, 2013 was passed. The Bill would amend that Act and the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 extensively, on the recommendations of the Company Law Committee (2022) and the High-Level Committee on Non-Financial Regulatory Reforms. Its central objective is to reduce compliance burdens and ensure proportionate enforcement without compromising the safeguards on which investor confidence depends. This paper asks how far such simplification can go before accountability suffers. The paper examines the decriminalisation of minor offences and their shift to electronic adjudication. It analyses ease of doing business measures, including virtual meetings, flexible buybacks, lower fast-track merger thresholds and a single NCLT bench. It further evaluates corporate governance reforms and new frameworks for IFSCs, trust-to-LLP conversion and employee compensation. The paper argues that simplification is justified only when it reduces procedural burdens without weakening essential safeguards. Several provisions, however, fall short of this standard in their present form. The Bill aims to promote ease of doing business and improve the operational efficiency of the two Acts, but what it achieves will depend on a coherent regulatory scheme and clear statutory drafting, supported by timely subordinate legislation.

title: An Integrated Framework for Enhancing Governance and Consequence Management in the South African Public Sector: Case of KwaZulu-Natal Provincial Administration
summary: Governance failures in the South African public sector persist despite the existence of extensive legislative and institutional frameworks. These failures are less a function of policy absence and more a consequence of weak implementation, fragmented accountability systems, and inconsistent enforcement of consequence management. This study develops and empirically grounds the Integrated Multi-Stakeholder Governance and Consequence Management Framework (IMGCF-KZN), using the KwaZulu-Natal Provincial Administration as a case. A convergent parallel mixed methods design was employed, combining quantitative data from 200 respondents with qualitative insights from 15 purposively selected governance practitioners. Statistical analysis revealed a significant relationship between good governance and consequence management, while corporate governance structures alone showed limited direct impact when not supported by enforcement and ethical leadership. The findings suggest that governance effectiveness depends on the integration of systems, stakeholder participation, and operational accountability mechanisms. The proposed framework introduces a multi-layered governance model comprising an enabling environment, six interdependent pillars, operational tools, and dynamic feedback loops. The study contributes to literature by shifting the focus from compliance-driven governance to enforcement-oriented and practice-based implementation. It further provides a practical model for strengthening systemwide accountability, improving institutional performance, ethical leadership, institutional transparency and integrity systems and restoring public trust in the South African public sector.

title: Reimagining Talent Management Practices in South African Municipality for a Future-Driven Public Workforce
summary: Municipalities in South Africa are increasingly pressured to reform their talent management practices amidst challenges such as skills shortages, digital transformation, and an ageing workforce. Traditional public sector human resource models are proving inadequate to meet the demands of a dynamic, future-driven service environment. There is a critical need to reimagine talent strategies that can build agile, competent, and future-ready public workforces.This study aimed to explore and evaluate current talent management practices within South African municipalities and to identify innovative, sustainable strategies that support workforce readiness for future public service demands. It specifically examined recruitment, retention, development, and strategic alignment of talent within the context of evolving governance and digital requirements. A qualitative research methodology was employed, using semi-structured interviews with 15 HR practitioners and senior municipal officials across selected municipalities. Data were analysed using thematic analysis, supported by NVivo software. The study was guided by the Strategic Human Resource Management (SHRM) theoretical framework and adhered to Lincoln and Guba’s criteria for trustworthiness. Findings reveal fragmented talent practices, limited succession planning, inadequate digital readiness, and minimal integration of future-focused competencies. However, initiatives such as continuous training, mentorship, inclusive recruitment, and e-governance integration were identified as potential levers for transformation. To build a resilient and high-performing municipal workforce, municipalities must adopt strategic, innovation-oriented talent management practices aligned with future-of-work paradigms. This study offers practical recommendations for aligning municipal HR practices with digital transformation, workforce renewal, and sustainable service delivery imperatives.

title: Attitudes and beliefs regarding future municipal eldercare needs: health and welfare technology or whom do I want support from when I need it?
summary: Introduction Our eldercare is undergoing a digital transformation, giving older adults new ways of receiving support. This study examined residents’ attitudes and beliefs about the future municipal provision of eldercare, focusing on the role of Health and Welfare Technology (HWT) in meeting these needs, using Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Methods A total of 979 residents aged 18–30, 31–64, and 65–84 years in Eskilstuna, Sweden, who responded to a survey 2024 about their attitudes toward eldercare in 2039, were included. The survey covered views on independence, use of HWT and sociodemographic factors. Descriptive methods and Pearson’s chi-square tests were used to describe independence, including variations in attitudes toward HWT by age and education level. Results Almost all respondents (96%) considered independence to be important, and a majority positive about the on-going digital transformation. More than half were open to receiving future municipal support via HWT. However, acceptance of HWT varied: those aged 65–84 were less positive (57%) compared to those aged 31–64 (65%). Still, about 30% of the oldest group preferred support by HWT for personal hygiene and night supervision. The attitudes also varied by educational level. Respondents with lower education were less supportive of HWT (49%) compared to those with higher education (65%). Nevertheless, 24–32% of those with lower education preferred HWT for personal hygiene and night supervision. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use may be important for positive attitudes to HWT, as proposed in TAM. Conclusion In summary, older adults and those with lower educational level had less positive attitudes towards future eldercare that may be provided by HWT, compared with middle-aged respondents and those with higher education. Although frailty was not assessed in this study, the findings may be relevant to frailty prevention because HWT may support independence, safety and functional ability in later life.

title: At the Edge of the State: Tax Law, AI and the Rise of Embedded Governance
summary: This study examines the digital transformation of tax administration in Sweden and Ukraine through a dynamic approach to comparative jurisprudence. By analyzing legal frameworks, institutional arrangements, and emerging GovTech practices, it moves beyond conventional comparisons of tax systems to investigate how data-driven ecosystems reshape administrative processes. The research highlights how both countriesdespite differing levels of economic development and digital maturityintegrate technological tools, platforms, and AI into their tax administrations. In doing so, the study addresses a comparatively underexplored pairing in tax scholarship and offers new insights into the relationship between technological innovation, regulatory design, and administrative capacity. The findings contribute to broader discussions on digital taxation, administrative modernization, and the evolving role of law in governing data-intensive public institutions.

title: Organizational and Economic Aspects of Increasing The Competitiveness of Service Enterprises Mechanisms
summary: The competitive advantage of service enterprises is vital for their success in modern market economies. Effective management of competitiveness through organizational and economic mechanisms is essential in maintaining long-term viability in a rapidly evolving market. This is particularly relevant in Uzbekistan's service sector, where globalization and technological advancements have intensified competition. Service enterprises must leverage strategic management, innovation, and resource optimization to gain and sustain competitive advantages. Although various theories exist on competitive advantage, including Porter's framework and the resource-based approach, a detailed analysis of integrated organizational, economic, and marketing mechanisms tailored to the service industry remains underexplored. This study aims to identify and evaluate the key strategies for enhancing the competitiveness of service enterprises in Uzbekistan. It explores how competitive advantages are formed through cost leadership, differentiation, and specialization strategies, focusing on the service sector's unique characteristics. The research highlights that integrating organizational, economic, and innovative mechanisms leads to sustainable competitive advantage. Key strategies such as cost optimization, service differentiation, and digital transformation were identified as critical factors in strengthening competitiveness. This study offers a comprehensive approach that incorporates modern management theories with industry-specific factors to develop effective competitive strategies for service enterprises. The findings suggest practical recommendations for service enterprises, including the adoption of flexible pricing systems, digital service enhancements, and workforce training. Further research could explore the application of these strategies in different regional contexts.

title: A Thematic Review of the Literature Pertaining to Industry 4.0 Implementation in Manufacturing MSMEs
summary: This article applies a systematic literature review approach to identify the dominant research themes in the literature on ‘Industry 4.0 adoption in manufacturing micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs)’. The review identifies six thematic areas: (a) barriers and enablers, (b) readiness and maturity models, (c) implementation frameworks, (d) technology applicability, (e) problem-specific applications and (f) impacts of technology adoption. The review highlights the preference of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in implementing low-cost solutions to address immediate operational challenges. These pragmatic experimentations of MSMEs often generate immediate economic and organizational benefits. However, the broader social and environmental outcomes are scantly reported. The study links the themes to established theories and highlights the need for more theory-driven, longitudinal and comparative research. By consolidating dispersed insights into a coherent framework, the review advances understanding of MSME digital transformation and outlines directions for future research, practice and policy.

title: Litigation risk, institutional ownership and corporate greenwashing
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how litigation risk affects corporate greenwashing among Chinese A-share listed non-financial firms from 2009 to 2022. It explores whether firms facing greater legal pressure adopt symbolic environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosure to preserve legitimacy and manage stakeholder perceptions. The study also investigates whether institutional ownership moderates this relationship and whether the effects differ across ownership structure and audit quality. Design/methodology/approach The analysis uses firm-level panel data regression models with firm, industry and year fixed effects. Multiple robustness tests are conducted to address endogeneity concerns and verify result consistency. The study further performs moderation analysis for institutional ownership and heterogeneity analysis for ownership structure and audit quality. Findings The results show that higher litigation risk significantly increases the likelihood of corporate greenwashing, indicating that legal pressure encourages symbolic rather than substantive ESG practices. Institutional ownership weakens this relationship, highlighting the monitoring role of institutional investors. The positive effect of litigation risk is stronger in non-state-owned enterprises and firms not audited by Big Four accounting firms. These results remain robust across alternative model specifications. Originality/value This study introduces litigation risk as a strategic driver of corporate greenwashing and extends legitimacy theory to the Chinese context. It demonstrates how legal pressure and governance mechanisms jointly shape firms’ ESG disclosure behavior. The findings offer new insights for regulators and investors aiming to strengthen ESG reporting standards, enhance enforcement and promote authentic sustainability practices in emerging markets.

title: Global decentralized stock exchange: an innovative permissioned-blockchain framework for integrated capital markets
summary: Purpose This paper aims to propose a regulatory-aware conceptual and theoretical framework for a global decentralized stock exchange built on a permissioned blockchain infrastructure. It examines how integrating trading, clearing, custody and supervisory functions within a unified distributed ledger can enhance efficiency, liquidity and compliance across jurisdictions. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a dual technical–regulatory framework supported by a reduced-form theoretical model grounded in market microstructure and governance theory. It evaluates consensus mechanisms, interoperability, privacy and scalability alongside consortium governance, cross-border oversight, legal recognition of tokenized securities and automated compliance, informed by comparisons with legacy exchanges and selected industry pilots. Findings Permissioned blockchain exchanges with atomic settlement and embedded compliance can reduce transaction costs, settlement risk and information asymmetries while improving liquidity, transparency and participation. The model predicts narrower spreads, higher trading volume and greater stability relative to conventional T+2 infrastructures. Practical implications The framework offers regulators, exchanges and financial institutions a phased implementation roadmap, governance templates and compliance-by-design mechanisms that enable gradual migration from legacy systems without sacrificing accountability or investor protection. Originality/value The paper introduces a hybrid governance model that embeds regulatory enforcement directly into exchange architecture and links design parameters to testable economic outcomes, advancing research at the intersection of financial regulation, fintech infrastructure and market microstructure.

title: FINANCIAL INCLUSION, DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND ENERGY CONSUMPTION DYNAMICS: EVIDENCE FROM OIC ECONOMIES
summary: This study examines the impact of digitalization and financial inclusion on energy consumption across 40 OIC member countries from 2001 to 2022. The research used several advanced panel econometric techniques, including cross-sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity tests, CIPS, IPS, and LLC unit root tests, Pedroni, Kao, and Westerlund cointegration tests, FMOLS and DOLS long-run estimators and the Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MMQR) approach. The findings indicate that digitalization and financial inclusion significantly reduce energy consumption in overall OIC countries and particularly in higher-income OIC countries by improving energy efficiency, facilitating technological innovation, and promoting the adoption of energy-efficient technologies. However, in lower-income OIC countries, digitalization and financial inclusion increase energy consumption due to increasing industrial activity, growing access to energy-dependent technologies, and rising economic participation. Furthermore, industrialization and population are found to increase energy consumption across all country groups. The interaction effect between Digitalization and financial inclusion indicates that their combined role contributes to energy sustainability, especially in higher-income OIC countries. The study highlights important policy implications for sustainable energy management in OIC economies. Policymakers should promote digital infrastructure, expand inclusive financial systems, and encourage green financing mechanisms to accelerate the adoption of energy-efficient technologies while ensuring sustainable energy transition pathways, particularly in lower-income OIC countries.

title: The Mediating Role of Technology Adoption Readiness on Computer-Based Human Resources Systems Usage among Manufacturing Small and Medium Enterprises in Harare
summary: Rampant digital transformation has ignited an inevitable new reality for Small and Medium Enterprises, and insufficient capacity, technological adoption readiness, and the underutilisation of Computer-Based Human Resources Systems have led to a high rate of business failure or closure in their first five years of operation. This study investigated the impact of Computer-Based Human Resources Systems, Technology Adoption Readiness, and Organisational Performance among Manufacturing Small and Medium Enterprises. The study focused on SMEs operating in Harare Metropolitan Province, Zimbabwe. A quantitative research approach was used, using data collected from 195 randomly selected respondents across 5 SMEs. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and linear regression techniques. The findings revealed that Technology Adoption Readiness significantly mediates the relationship between CBHR systems and organisational performance, and CBHR systems positively contribute to enhanced performance. SMEs with higher levels of technology adoption readiness demonstrated improved performance in dynamic business environments. The study concludes that CBHR systems play a crucial role in firm performance and that technology adoption readiness also serves as an intermediary, strengthening the impact of CBHR systems on SME performance in Zimbabwe. The study contributes to the inadequate literature on the impact of Computer-Based Human Resources Systems, Technology Adoption Readiness, and Organisational Performance by empirically demonstrating the mediating role of Technology Adoption Readiness and the impact of CBHR systems. To promote enhanced performance in SMEs, the findings provide practical insights for policymakers and SME managers.

title: Does environmental judicial reform influence audit fees? Evidence from China's environmental public interest litigation
summary: Purpose A careful study of the impact of the environmental public interest litigation (EPIL) pilot policy on audit fees would not only make the economic costs of judicial innovation in environmental governance but also the study would make a strong empirical statement about improving the environmental practices of the business community and audit policies. Design/methodology/approach We are working with a quasi-natural experiment in China based on its EPIL pilot program and we apply a difference-in-differences framework. Findings We find that firms in pilot regions pay 4.7% higher audit fees than non-pilot peers, a result robust to parallel-trend checks, placebo tests, propensity score matching and controls for concurrent policies. Mechanism evidence indicates that the EPIL pilot policy elevates auditors' perceived litigation and regulatory risk, leading to higher risk premia in pricing without commensurate increases in engagement hours. Effects are stronger for firms with weaker ESG, greater information asymmetry, higher auditor specialization, lower auditor workload pressure, or strong regional environmental policy enforcement. Further analysis shows that the increase in audit fees associated with the EPIL pilot policy does not lead to an improvement in audit quality. Originality/value (1) Incorporating bottom-up judicial environmental regulation (EPIL) into audit pricing frameworks, filling a research gap, (2) developing a unified auditor-auditee strategic interaction framework that reveals how external policies affect audit fee equilibrium through risk-sharing and resource allocation and (3) systematically explicating the transmission mechanism from environmental legal risks to audit risk premiums, enriching audit pricing theory.

title: The evolution of legitimacy discourse in corporate social responsibility reporting: evidence from a state-owned Irish energy company (2003-2025)
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how legitimacy is discursively constructed and stabilised over time in corporate social responsibility (CSR) reporting in a state-owned enterprise (SOE) and what these legitimacy dynamics reveal about how an SOE responds to evolving sustainable-development expectations. Design/methodology/approach The CSR sections of the Electricity Supply Board’s annual reports from 2003 to 2025 are analysed using a theory-informed computerised content analysis based on Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count categories mapped to Suchman’s (1995) legitimacy framework. To assess the mapping’s interpretive validity, the authors incorporate several robustness analyses. Findings Over the 23-year period studied, the reports increasingly and consistently used language that conveyed a sense of the ESB as a natural, accepted part of everyday life. While the report language reflected pragmatic and moral legitimacy, cognitive legitimacy was prominent. This prominence is observed across multiple analytical approaches, suggesting a stable discursive orientation. This finding suggests that in SOE contexts, legitimacy depends less on actively persuading stakeholders and more on being perceived as taken-for-granted in society. Sustainable-development transitions occur through organisations whose historically embedded societal roles can both support continuity and require continuing accountability as sustainable-development expectations change. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on a single case. Also, the operationalisation of legitimacy through linguistic proxies involves interpretive judgement. While robustness checks provide support for the findings, the results should be understood as indicative patterns, not precise measurements. Practical implications The findings highlight CSR reporting as a component of managing long-term legitimacy, particularly for publicly accountable organisations. Managers may draw on historically embedded narratives and societal connections to enhance trust and alignment with sustainable-development expectations. Social implications For policymakers and regulators, the findings suggest that sustainability reporting is more than a compliance exercise – it is part of a wider infrastructure supporting public accountability and long-term societal value, and this should inform how reporting is designed. For organisations, actively cultivating a sense of being a trusted part of society through reporting can strengthen stakeholder ties and support broader sustainable development efforts. Originality/value This study provides longitudinal evidence on the configuration of legitimacy forms in CSR reporting, showing that legitimacy dynamics in SOEs differ from prior literature and the relevance of historically accumulated legitimacy to sustainable development. It also contributes methodologically by proxying legitimacy types to automated text analysis.

title: A Method-Derived Framework for Evidence-Based Sustainability Reporting Education: Environmental Materiality, ESG Literacy and Colombian Manufacturing
summary: This study examines how corporate sustainability reports and official environmental statistics can be combined analytically to support a conceptual framework for sustainability education, ESG literacy, environmental accounting, and professional training in business, management, and engineering programs. Focusing on Colombian manufacturing, the study triangulates GRI-coded corporate disclosures with sector-level indicators on waste generation, water use, and environmental investment. The findings identify strong structural alignment for water-related disclosure, partial alignment for waste and emissions themes, and recurrent emphasis on governance and social topics that are weakly connected to the selected environmental-pressure indicators. On the basis of this analytical sequence, the article proposes a method-derived pedagogical framework for critically comparing sustainability narratives with external evidence. The framework was not tested as an educational intervention: no students, instructors, courses, comparison conditions, or learning outcomes were evaluated. Accordingly, the educational contribution should be interpreted as a conceptually grounded application of the research method rather than evidence of demonstrated teaching effectiveness.
